arc_intro:
FQ-171 — Ravi Krishnan (Head of Engineering)

One more thing before we move past compute: I keep hearing that order-service's instances are reachable directly, bypassing whatever load balancing we have. Go check whether that's actually true, and if it is, let's understand exactly why and fix it properly — target groups, health checks, all of it.

— Ravi
arc_outro:
Ravi Krishnan — FQ-171 update:

Turns out I had the details slightly wrong, but the underlying worry was right — there IS an ALB already, but the instances' security group never actually restricted access to just it, so they were reachable directly the whole time regardless. Good catch fixing that, and good catch on the health check path mismatch too, which was quietly making the ALB think healthy instances were unhealthy.

Next: let's talk about scaling itself. Right now this fleet grows and shrinks based on someone noticing, not on any automatic policy. Let's fix that.

— Ravi

tasks.question: What's the core difference between an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and a Network Load Balancer (NLB)?
options: A) They're functionally identical, just with different names and pricing

B) ALB operates at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS), enabling path-based and host-based routing decisions based on the actual request content. NLB operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), offering extremely low latency and a static IP, but without any awareness of HTTP-level content like paths or headers
C) NLB is simply a cheaper, older version of ALB with fewer features but otherwise identical behavior
D) ALB can only be used with EC2, while NLB can only be used with Lambda

tasks.scenario: Continuing the audit, you pull the full current state of order-service's load balancing setup.
tasks.broken_config:
Application Load Balancer: foodquick-order-alb
├── Listener: HTTPS:443 → forwards to order-service-tg

Target group: order-service-tg
├── Health check path: /healthcheck
├── Health check interval: 30s
├── Healthy threshold: 3 consecutive successes
├── Unhealthy threshold: 3 consecutive failures
└── Registered targets: 4 instances, ALL currently marked UNHEALTHY

Actual order-service application:
└── Serves its health endpoint at /health (not /healthcheck) — confirmed by checking the application's own routing code

Instance security group (sg-order-svc-0072):
└── Inbound: Port 80, 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 (not restricted to the ALB's security group)
what_to_find: The health check path (/healthcheck) doesn't match what the application actually serves (/health) — every health check request gets a 404, so ALL targets are marked unhealthy even though the application itself is running fine
Because all targets are marked unhealthy, the ALB has effectively nowhere healthy to route traffic — this could cause real customer-facing failures despite the application working correctly

Separately, the instance security group allows direct inbound access from 0.0.0.0/0 on the same ports the ALB uses, meaning anyone can bypass the ALB (and its health-check-based protection) entirely and hit an instance directly
These are two independent problems that happen to compound each other — even if the health check were fixed, direct access would still be an open security gap, and vice versa
tasks.correct_fix: Fix the health check path in the target group to /health, matching what the application actually serves. Separately, update sg-order-svc-0072 to restrict inbound on 80/443 to ONLY the ALB's security group, removing the 0.0.0.0/0 rule entirely.

tasks.question: Is using the ALB's current IP addresses as the security group source a good approach?
options: A) Yes — IP addresses are the most precise and permanent way to restrict access

B) No — ALBs can have their underlying IP addresses change over time (AWS manages this transparently), so hardcoding them is fragile. The correct approach is referencing the ALB's SECURITY GROUP ID as the source, which stays valid regardless of any underlying IP changes
C) Yes, but only if the IPs are updated manually every 24 hours
D) It doesn't matter, since ALBs never change their IP addresses once created

tasks.scenario: Right after restricting the security group (before the health check fix is deployed), you briefly see the ALB's CloudWatch metrics show a spike in 5xx errors, and initially suspect the SG change broke something.
tasks.error_shown: ALB Target Group logs: "Health checks failed with 404: GET /healthcheck" (this exact error was ALREADY present before the SG change, just not as visible since direct-access traffic was masking the impact)
tasks.diagnosis: The 5xx spike coincided with the SG change but was NOT caused by it — investigating the actual target group logs shows the /healthcheck 404 errors were already happening continuously beforehand. What likely changed is that with direct access now blocked, ALL traffic is forced through the ALB, which was ALREADY relying on its fail-open behavior for all-unhealthy targets — removing the direct-access "safety valve" (however unintentional and insecure it was) made the ALB's fragile fail-open routing the only path, and any brief hiccup in that fallback behavior became immediately visible as 5xx errors to customers.
tasks.fix: Deploy the health check path fix (/healthcheck → /health) immediately — this addresses the actual root cause. Once targets report healthy correctly, the ALB routes normally and stops relying on fail-open behavor entirely, resolving the 5xx spike properly rather than coincidentally.

cases.case_1: A new customer-facing API that needs path-based routing (e.g. /api/orders vs /api/users going to different target groups) and SSL termination
cases.case_2: A new internal gRPC-based service between two backend systems that needs the lowest possible latency and doesn't need any HTTP-level routing logic
cases.case_3: A service that needs a static IP address for allowlisting purposes with an external partner's firewall

correct_answers.case_1: ALB — path-based routing and SSL termination are exactly ALB's Layer 7 strengths
correct_answers.case_2: NLB — Layer 4 raw performance with minimal overhead fits low-latency gRPC/TCP traffic better than ALB's HTTP-aware processing
correct_answers.case_3: NLB — NLB supports static IP addresses (or Elastic IPs) per AZ, which ALB does not offer in the same way, making it the right fit when a partner needs to allowlist a fixed IP

tasks.scenario: Ravi asks about the real risk exposure the direct-access gap represented, for the incident writeup. FoodQuick's order-service handles customer payment initiation; a comparable direct-access bypass at a similar-sized Indian company led to a documented ₹6.2 lakh fraud loss last year when attackers found and hit an origin server directly, bypassing the load balancer's request logging and any WAF rules attached to it.
tasks.question: How should the risk (not just the fix) be communicated in the report, given nothing bad actually happened this time?
tasks.solution: Frame it accurately: nothing was exploited THIS time, but the gap existed for an unknown period and bypassed every protection normally sitting in front of the ALB (request logging, any future WAF rules, DDoS protections). The ₹6.2 lakh comparable incident illustrates the realistic scale of what this class of gap can cost when it IS found and exploited — not a claim that FoodQuick specifically lost money, but a concrete reason this deserved priority even though this specific instance turned out fine.
tasks.explanation: This real risk communication — 'nothing happened, so no big deal' — underplay do not, 'we got breached' — overclaim to do vendaam. Comparable incident's real number giving, scale-a honestly convey for doing help does.
